entries.489b171a43cb386a443434ba56c0a90563a2668b: <div sID="gen5401" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="1Sam.9" sID="1Sam.9"/> <div eID="gen5401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5402" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5403" type="x-p"/> Samuel had promised Israel, from God, that they should have a king; it is strange that the next news is not of candidates setting up for the government, making an interest in the people, or recommending themselves to Samuel, and, by him, to God, to be put in nomination. Why does not the prince of the tribe of Judah, whoever he is, look about him now, remembering Jacob's entail of the sceptre on that tribe? Is there never a bold aspiring man in Israel, to say, "I will be king, if God will choose me?" No, none appears, whether it is owing to a culpable mean-spiritedness or a laudable humility I know not; but surely it is what can scarcely be paralleled in the history of any kingdom; a crown, such a crown, set up, and nobody bids for it. Most governments began in the ambition of the prince to rule, but Israel's in the ambition of the people to be ruled. Had any of those elders who petitioned for a king afterwards petitioned to be king, I should have suspected that person's ambition to have been at the bottom of the motion; but now (let them have the praise of what was good in them) it was not so. God having, in the law, undertaken to choose their king (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.15">Deut. xvii. 15</reference>), they all sit still, till they hear from heaven, and that they do in this chapter, which begins the story of Saul, their first king, and, by strange steps of Providence, brings him to Samuel to be anointed privately, and so to be prepared for an election by lot, and a public commendation to the people, which follows in the next chapter. Here is, I. A short account of Saul's parentage and person, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1-1Sam.9.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. A large and particular account of the bringing of him to Samuel, to whom he had been before altogether a stranger. 1. God, by revelation, had told Samuel to expect him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15-1Sam.9.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. 2. God, by providence, led him to Samuel. (1.) Being sent to seek his father's asses, he was at a loss, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.3-1Sam.9.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. (2.) By the advice of his servant, he determined to consult Samuel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6-1Sam.9.10">ver. 6-10</reference>. (3.) By the direction of the young maidens, he found him out, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.11-1Sam.9.14">ver. 11-14</reference>. (4.) Samuel, being informed of God concerning him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.17">ver. 17</reference>), treated him with respect in the gate (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.18-1Sam.9.21">ver. 18-21</reference>), in the dining-room (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.22">ver. 22-24</reference>), and at length in private, where he prepared him to hear the surprising news that he must be king, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.25-1Sam.9.27">ver. 25-27</reference>. And these beginnings would have been very hopeful and promising if it had not been that the sin of the people was the spring of this great affair.
entries.49fbff32271a239ed2bd51c28fea959bdd2f47e6: <div eID="gen5403" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5402" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parentage of Saul. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1075.)</title> <div sID="gen5404" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bechorath, the son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, a mighty man of power. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he had a son, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and <hi type="italic">there was</hi> not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward <hi type="italic">he was</hi> higher than any of the people. <div eID="gen5404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5405" type="x-p"/> We are here told, 1. What a good family Saul was of, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">v. 1</reference>. He was of the tribe of Benjamin; so was the New-Testament Saul, who also was called <hi type="italic">Paul,</hi> and he mentions it as his honour, for Benjamin was a favourite, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom. xi. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.5">Phil. iii. 5</reference>. That tribe had been reduced to a very small number by the fatal war with Gibeah, and much ado there was to provide wives for those 600 men that were the poor remains of it out of that diminished tribe, which is here called, with good reason, <hi type="italic">the smallest of the tribes of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.21">v. 21</reference>. Saul sprang as a root out of a dry ground. That tribe, though fewest in number, was first in dignity, <hi type="italic">God giving more abundant honour to that part which lacked,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.24">1 Cor. xii. 24</reference>. His father was <hi type="italic">Kish, a mighty man of power,</hi> or, as the margin reads it, <hi type="italic">in substance;</hi> in spirit bold, in body strong, in estate wealthy. The whole lot of the tribe of Benjamin coming to be distributed among 600 men, we may suppose their inheritances were much larger than theirs who were of other tribes, an advantage which somewhat helped to balance the disadvantage of the smallness of their number. 2. What a good figure Saul made, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.2">v. 2</reference>. No mention is here made of his wisdom or virtue, his learning or piety, or any of the accomplishments of his mind, but that he was a tall, proper, handsome man, that had a good face, a good shape, and a good presence, graceful and well proportioned: <hi type="italic">Among all the children of Israel there was not a goodlier person than he;</hi> and, as if nature had marked him for pre-eminence and superiority, he was taller by the head and shoulders than any of the people, the fitter to be a match for the giants of Gath, the champions of the Philistines. When God chose a king after his own heart he pitched upon one that was not at all remarkable for the height of his stature, nor any thing in his countenance but the innocence and sweetness that appeared there, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.7">ch. xvi. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.12">12</reference>. But when he chose a king after the people's heart, who aimed at nothing so much as stateliness and grandeur, he pitched upon this huge tall man, who, if he had no other good qualities, yet would look great. It does not appear that he excelled in strength so much as he did in stature; Samson did, and him they slighted, bound, and betrayed into the hands of the Philistines; justly therefore are they now put off with one who, though of uncommon height, is weak as other men. They would have a king like the nations, and the nations commonly chose portly men for their kings.
entries.fe456b46c66032f10c02ac48604a0c49169321a0: <div eID="gen5405" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Seeks His Father's Asses; Saul Goes to Seek Samuel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1075.)</title> <div sID="gen5406" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> And the asses of Kish Saul's father were lost. And Kish said to Saul his son, Take now one of the servants with thee, and arise, go seek the asses. <hi type="super">4</hi> And he passed through mount Ephraim, and passed through the land of Shalisha, but they found <hi type="italic">them</hi> not: then they passed through the land of Shalim, and <hi type="italic">there they were</hi> not: and he passed through the land of the Benjamites, but they found <hi type="italic">them</hi> not. <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> when they were come to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant that <hi type="italic">was</hi> with him, Come, and let us return; lest my father leave <hi type="italic">caring</hi> for the asses, and take thought for us. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he said unto him, Behold now, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> in this city a man of God, and <hi type="italic">he is</hi> a honourable man; all that he saith cometh surely to pass: now let us go thither; peradventure he can shew us our way that we should go. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then said Saul to his servant, But, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> we go, what shall we bring the man? for the bread is spent in our vessels, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> not a present to bring to the man of God: what have we? <hi type="super">8</hi> And the servant answered Saul again, and said, Behold, I have here at hand the fourth part of a shekel of silver: <hi type="italic">that</hi> will I give to the man of God, to tell us our way. <hi type="super">9</hi> (Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> now <hi type="italic">called</hi> a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.) <hi type="super">10</hi> Then said Saul to his servant, Well said; come, let us go. So they went unto the city where the man of God <hi type="italic">was.</hi> <div eID="gen5406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5407" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A great man rising from small beginnings. It does not appear that Saul had any preferment at all, or was in any post of honour or trust, till he was chosen king of Israel. Most that are advanced rise gradually, but Saul, from the level with his neighbours, stepped at once into the throne, according to that of Hannah, He <hi type="italic">raiseth up the poor out of the dust, to set them among princes,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1 Sam. ii. 8</reference>. Saul, it should seem, though he was himself married and had children grown up, yet lived in his father's house, and was subject to him. Promotion comes not by chance nor human probabilities, but God is the Judge. <div eID="gen5407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5408" type="x-p"/> II. A great event arising from small occurrences. How low does the history begin! Having to trace Saul to the crown, we find him first employed as meanly as any we meet with called out to preferment. <div eID="gen5408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5409" type="x-p"/> 1. Saul's father sends him with one of his servants to seek some asses that he had lost. It may be they had no way then to give public notice of such a number of asses strayed or stolen out of the grounds of Kish the Benjamite. A very good law they had to oblige men to bring back an ox or an ass that went astray, but it is to be feared that was, as other good laws, neglected and forgotten. It is easy to observe here that those who have must expect to lose, that it is wisdom to look after what is lost, that no man should think it below him to know the state of his flocks, that children should be forward to serve their parents' interests. Saul readily went to <hi type="italic">seek his father's asses,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.3-1Sam.9.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. His taking care of the asses is to be ascribed, not so much to the humility of his spirit as to the plainness and simplicity of those times. But his obedience to his father in it was very commendable. <hi type="italic">Seest thou a man diligent in his business,</hi> and dutiful to his superiors, willing to stoop and willing to take pains? he does as Saul stand fair for preferment. The servant of Kish would be faithful only as a servant, but Saul as a son, in his own business, and therefore he was sent with him. Saul and his servants travelled far (probably on foot) in quest of the asses, but in vain: they found them not. He missed of what he sought, but had no reason to complain of the disappointment, for he met with the kingdom, which he never dreamed of. <div eID="gen5409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5410" type="x-p"/> 2. When he could not find them, he determined to return to his father (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.5">v. 5</reference>), in consideration of his father's tender concern for him, being apprehensive that if they staid out any longer his aged father would begin to fear, as Jacob concerning Joseph, that an evil beast had devoured them or some mischief had befallen them; he will <hi type="italic">leave caring for the asses,</hi> as much as he was in care about them, and <hi type="italic">will take thought for us.</hi> Children should take care that they do nothing to grieve or frighten their parents, but be tender of their tenderness. <div eID="gen5410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5411" type="x-p"/> 3. His servant proposed (for, it should seem, he had more religion in him than his master) that, since they were now at Ramah, they should call on Samuel, and take his advice in this important affair. Observe here, (1.) They were close by the city where Samuel lived, and that put it into their heads to consult him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is in this city a man of God.</hi> Note, Wherever we are we should improve our opportunities of acquainting ourselves with those that are wise and good. But there are many that will consult a man of God, if he comes in their way, that would not go a step out of their way to get wisdom. (2.) The servant spoke very respectfully concerning Samuel, though he had not personal knowledge of him, but by common fame only: <hi type="italic">He is a man of God, and an honourable man.</hi> Note, Men of God are honourable men, and should be so in our eyes. Acquaintance with the things of God, and serviceableness to the kingdom of God, put true honour upon men, and make them great. This was the honour of Samuel, as a man of God, that <hi type="italic">all he saith comes surely to pass.</hi> This was observed concerning him when he was a young prophet (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.19">ch. iii. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">God did let none of his words fall to the ground;</hi> and still it held true. (3.) They agreed to consult him concerning <hi type="italic">the way that they should go; peradventure he can show us.</hi> All the use they would make of the man of God was to be advised by him whether they should return home, or, if there were any hopes of finding the asses, which way they must go next—a poor business to employ a prophet about! Had they said, "Let us give up the asses for lost, and, now that we are so near the man of God, let us go and learn from him the good knowledge of God, let us consult him how we may order our conversations a right, and enquire the law at his mouth, since we may not have such another opportunity, and then we shall not lose our journey"—the proposal would have been such as became Israelites; but to make prophecy, that glory of Israel, serve so mean a turn as this, discovered too much what manner of spirit they were of. Note, Most people would rather be told their fortune than told their duty, how to be rich than how to be saved. If it were the business of the men of God to direct for the recovery of lost asses, they would be consulted much more than they are now that it is their business to direct for the recovery of lost souls; so preposterous is the care of most men! (4.) Saul was thoughtful what present they should bring to the man of God, what fee they should give him for his advice (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">What shall we bring the man?</hi> They could not present him, as Jeroboam's wife did Ahijah, with loaves and cakes (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.3">1 Kings xiv. 3</reference>), for their bread was spent; but the servant bethought himself that he had in his pocket the fourth part of a shekel, about seven-pence halfpenny in value, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> he would give to the man of God to direct them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.8">v. 8</reference>. "That will do," says Saul; "<hi type="italic">let us go,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.10">v. 10</reference>. Some think that when Saul talked of giving Samuel a fee he measured him by himself, or by his sons, as if he must be hired to do an honest Israelite a kindness, and was like the false prophets, that <hi type="italic">divined for money,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mic. iii. 11</reference>. He came to him as a fortune-teller, rather than as a prophet, and therefore thought the fourth part of a shekel was enough to give him. But it rather seems to be agreeable to the general usage of those times, as it is to natural equity, that those who sowed spiritual things should reap not only eternal things from him that employs them, but temporal things from those for whom they are employed. Samuel needed not their money, nor would he have denied them his advice if they had not brought it (it is probable, when he had it, he gave it to the poor); but they brought it to him as a token of their respect and the value they put upon his office; nor did he refuse it, for they were able to give it, and, though it was but little, it was the widow's mite. But Saul, as he never thought of going to the man of God till the servant proposed it, so, it should seem, he mentioned the want of a present as an objection against their going; he would not own that he had money in his pocket, but, when the servant generously offered to be at the charge, then, "Well, said," says Saul; "come, let us go." Most people love a cheap religion, and like it best when they can devolve the expense of it on others. (5.) The historian here takes notice of the name then given to the prophets: they called them <hi type="italic">Seers,</hi> or <hi type="italic">seeing men</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.9">v. 9</reference>), not but that the name <hi type="italic">prophet</hi> was then used, and applied to such persons, but that of seers was more in use. Note, Those that are prophets must first be seers; those who undertake to speak to others of the things of God must have an insight into those things themselves.
entries.31c70b709d819f4501f48de6c9380e3acd0d559d: <div eID="gen5411" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Introduced to Samuel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1070.)</title> <div sID="gen5412" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> as they went up the hill to the city, they found young maidens going out to draw water, and said unto them, Is the seer here? <hi type="super">12</hi> And they answered them, and said, He is; behold, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> before you: make haste now, for he came to day to the city; for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a sacrifice of the people to day in the high place: <hi type="super">13</hi> As soon as ye be come into the city, ye shall straightway find him, before he go up to the high place to eat: for the people will not eat until he come, because he doth bless the sacrifice; <hi type="italic">and</hi> afterwards they eat that be bidden. Now therefore get you up; for about this time ye shall find him. <hi type="super">14</hi> And they went up into the city: <hi type="italic">and</hi> when they were come into the city, behold, Samuel came out against them, for to go up to the high place. <hi type="super">15</hi> Now the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had told Samuel in his ear a day before Saul came, saying, <hi type="super">16</hi> To morrow about this time I will send thee a man out of the land of Benjamin, and thou shalt anoint him <hi type="italic">to be</hi> captain over my people Israel, that he may save my people out of the hand of the Philistines: for I have looked upon my people, because their cry is come unto me. <hi type="super">17</hi> And when Samuel saw Saul, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto him, Behold the man whom I spake to thee of! this same shall reign over my people. <div eID="gen5412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5413" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Saul, by an ordinary enquiry, is directed to Samuel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.11-1Sam.9.14">v. 11-14</reference>. Gibeah of Saul was not twenty miles from Ramah where Samuel dwelt, and was near to Mizpeh where he often judged Israel, and yet, it seems, Saul had lived so very privately, and had taken so little notice of public affairs, that he had never seen Samuel, for when he met him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.18">v. 18</reference>) he did not know him, so that there was no cause to suspect any secret compact or collusion between them in this matter. <hi type="italic">I knew him not,</hi> says John Baptist concerning Christ, <reference osisRef="John.1.31">John i. 31</reference>. Yet I do not think it any commendation to Saul that he was a stranger to Samuel. However, <div eID="gen5413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5414" type="x-p"/> 1. The maid-servants of Ramah, whom they met with at the places of drawing water, could give him and his servant intelligence concerning Samuel; and very particular they were in their directions, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.12-1Sam.9.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. We should always be ready to give what assistance we can to those that are enquiring after God's prophets, and to further them in their enquiries. Even the maid-servants could tell them, (1.) That there was a sacrifice that day in the high place, it being either an ordinary festival or an extraordinary day of prayer and thanksgiving, with which sacrifices were joined. The tabernacle being deprived of the ark, the altar there had not now the reputation it formerly had, nor were they confined to it, as they would be when God had again chosen a place to put his name in; and therefore now other places were allowed. Samuel had built an altar at Ramah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.17">ch. vii. 17</reference>), and here we have him making use of that altar. (2.) That Samuel came that day to the city, either from his circuit or from his country seat. He was such a public person that his movements were generally known. (3.) That this was just the time of their meeting to feast before the Lord upon the sacrifice: "About this time you will find him in the street going up to the high place." They knew the hour of the solemn feast. (4.) That the people would not eat till Samuel came, not only because he was the worthiest person, and they ought in good manners to stay for him, and he was, as some think, the maker of this feast, the sacrifice being offered at his charge and upon his account; but because, as a man of God, whoever made the feast, <hi type="italic">he</hi> must bless the sacrifice, that is, those parts of the sacrifice which they feasted upon, which may be considered, [1.] As a common meal, and so this is an instance of the great duty of craving a blessing upon our meat before we partake of it. We cannot expect benefit from our food without that blessing, and we have no reason to expect that blessing if we do not pray for it. Thus we must give glory to God as our benefactor, and own our dependence upon him and our obligations to him. Or, [2.] As a religious assembly. When the sacrifice was offered, which was the ceremony, Samuel blessed it, that is, he prayed over it, and offered up spiritual sacrifices with it, which were the substance; and afterwards, when the holy duties were performed, they did eat. Let the soul first be served. The feast upon the sacrifice being a sacred rite, it was requisite that it should in a particular manner be blessed, as is the Christian eucharist. They feasted in token of their reconciliation to God by virtue of the sacrifice, and their participation of the benefits of it; and Samuel blessed the feast, that is, he prayed to God to grace the solemnity with his special presence, that it might answer those great ends. Bishop Hall observes what a particular account those maid-servants could give of the usages of those sacred feasts, and infers from it that, "where there is the practice and example of piety in the better sort, there will be a reflection of it upon the meanest. It is no small advantage to live in religious places; for we shall be much to blame if all goodness fall beside us." <div eID="gen5414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5415" type="x-p"/> 2. Saul and his servant followed the directions given them, and very opportunely met Samuel going to the high place, the synagogue of the city, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.14">v. 14</reference>. This seemed purely accidental, but the divine providence ordered it for the forwarding of this great event. The wise God serves very great and certain purposes by very small and casual occurrences. A sparrow falls not to the ground without our Father. <div eID="gen5415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5416" type="x-p"/> II. Samuel, by an extraordinary revelation, is informed concerning Saul. He was a seer, and therefore must see this in a way peculiar to himself. <div eID="gen5416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5417" type="x-p"/> 1. God had told him, the day before, that he would, at this time, send him the man that should serve the people of Israel for such a king as they wished to have, <hi type="italic">like all the nations,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15-1Sam.9.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. He <hi type="italic">told him in his ear,</hi> that is, privately, by a secret whisper to his mind, or perhaps by a still small voice, some soft and gentle sounds conveyed to his ear, probably when he was praying in secret for direction in that and other affairs of the nation. He had spoken <hi type="italic">in the ears of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.21">ch. viii. 21</reference>), and now God <hi type="italic">spoke in his ear,</hi> in token of friendship and familiarity, for <hi type="italic">he revealeth his secret to his servants the prophets,</hi> as secrets in their ear, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">Amos iii. 7</reference>. God told him before, that it might not be a surprise to him; and perhaps it was in expectation of it that he appointed the feast and the sacrifice, for the imploring of God's blessing upon this great and important affair, though he might keep the particular occasion in his own breast, God having only told it to him in his ear. The Hebrew phrase is, <hi type="italic">He uncovered the ear of Samuel,</hi> to which some allude for the explication of the way of God's revealing himself to us; he not only speaks, but <hi type="italic">uncovers our ear.</hi> We have naturally a covering on our ears, so that we perceive not what God says (<reference osisRef="Job.33.14">Job xxxiii. 14</reference>), but, when God will manifest himself to a soul, he uncovers the ear, says, <hi type="italic">Ephphratha, Be opened;</hi> he takes <hi type="italic">the veil from off the heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.16">2 Cor. iii. 16</reference>. Though God had, in displeasure, granted their request for a king, yet here he speaks tenderly of Israel; for even in <hi type="italic">wrath he remembers mercy.</hi> (1.) He calls them again and again his people; though a peevish and provoking people, yet mine still. (2.) He sends them a man to be captain over them, that they might not be a body without a head, and to <hi type="italic">save them out of the hand of the Philistines,</hi> which perhaps was more than many of them aimed at in desiring a king. (3.) He does it with a gracious respect to them and to their cry: <hi type="italic">I have looked upon my people,</hi> and <hi type="italic">their cry has come unto me.</hi> He gratified them with what they cried for, as the tender mother humours the froward child, lest it should break its heart. And (as bishop Patrick observes), though he would not hear their cry to relieve them against the oppression of their kings (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.18">ch. viii. 18</reference>), yet he was so gracious as to make those kings instruments of their deliverance from the oppression of their neighbours, which was more than they had reason to expect. <div eID="gen5417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5418" type="x-p"/> 2. When Saul came up towards him in the street God again whispered Samuel in the ear (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold the man whom I spoke to thee of!</hi> Saul being a man of unusual stature, it is natural to think that Samuel fixed his eye upon him at a distance, and perhaps looked the more wistfully towards him because the hour had now come when God would send him the man that should be king of Israel, and he fancied this might be he; but, that he might be fully satisfied, God told him expressly, <hi type="italic">That is the man</hi> that shall <hi type="italic">restrain</hi> (for magistrates are heirs of restraint) <hi type="italic">my people Israel.</hi>
entries.645981420654077981a080338b43d55aac09c4f7: <div eID="gen5418" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Entertained by Samuel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1070.)</title> <div sID="gen5419" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Then Saul drew near to Samuel in the gate, and said, Tell me, I pray thee, where the seer's house <hi type="italic">is.</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> And Samuel answered Saul, and said, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the seer: go up before me unto the high place; for ye shall eat with me to day, and to morrow I will let thee go, and will tell thee all that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in thine heart. <hi type="super">20</hi> And as for thine asses that were lost three days ago, set not thy mind on them; for they are found. And on whom <hi type="italic">is</hi> all the desire of Israel? <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> not on thee, and on all thy father's house? <hi type="super">21</hi> And Saul answered and said, <hi type="italic">Am</hi> not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? wherefore then speakest thou so to me? <hi type="super">22</hi> And Samuel took Saul and his servant, and brought them into the parlour, and made them sit in the chiefest place among them that were bidden, which <hi type="italic">were</hi> about thirty persons. <hi type="super">23</hi> And Samuel said unto the cook, Bring the portion which I gave thee, of which I said unto thee, Set it by thee. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the cook took up the shoulder, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> which <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon it, and set <hi type="italic">it</hi> before Saul. And <hi type="italic">Samuel</hi> said, Behold that which is left! set <hi type="italic">it</hi> before thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> eat: for unto this time hath it been kept for thee since I said, I have invited the people. So Saul did eat with Samuel that day. <hi type="super">25</hi> And when they were come down from the high place into the city, <hi type="italic">Samuel</hi> communed with Saul upon the top of the house. <hi type="super">26</hi> And they arose early: and it came to pass about the spring of the day, that Samuel called Saul to the top of the house, saying, Up, that I may send thee away. And Saul arose, and they went out both of them, he and Samuel, abroad. <hi type="super">27</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> as they were going down to the end of the city, Samuel said to Saul, Bid the servant pass on before us, (and he passed on,) but stand thou still a while, that I may shew thee the word of God. <div eID="gen5419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5420" type="x-p"/> Providence having at length brought Samuel and Saul together, we have here an account of what passed between them in the gate, at the feast, and in private. <div eID="gen5420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5421" type="x-p"/> I. In the gate of the city; passing through that, Saul found him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.18">v. 18</reference>), and, little thinking that he was Samuel himself, asked him the way to Samuel's house: <hi type="italic">Tell me where the seer's house is;</hi> for there he expected to find him. See how mean a figure Samuel made, though so great a man: he took not any state, had no attendants, no ensigns of honour carried before him, nor any distinguishing habit, no, not when he went to church, but appeared, in all respects, so much a common person that Saul, though he was told he should meet him, never suspected that it was he, but, as if he looked more like a porter than a prophet, asked him the way to the seer's house. Thus is great worth oftentimes hidden under a very despicable appearance. Samuel knew that it was not the house, but the man, that he wanted, and therefore answered him, "<hi type="italic">I am the seer,</hi> the person you enquire for," <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.19">v. 19</reference>. Samuel knew him before he knew Samuel; thus, though all that are called to the kingdom of glory are brought to know God, yet first they were known of him, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Gal. iv. 9</reference>. Now, 1. Samuel obliges him to stay with him till the next day. The greatest part of this day had been spent in sacrificing, and the rest of it was to be spent in holy feasting, and therefore, "<hi type="italic">To-morrow I will let thee go,</hi> and not sooner; now <hi type="italic">go up before me to the high place;</hi> let us pray together, and then we will talk together." Saul had nothing in his mind but to find his asses, but Samuel would take him off from that care, and dispose him to the exercises of piety; and therefore bids him <hi type="italic">go to the high place,</hi> and go before him, because, it may be, some business obliged Samuel to call by the way. 2. He satisfies him about his asses (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Set not thy mind on them,</hi> be not in further care about them; <hi type="italic">they are found.</hi> By this Saul might perceive that he was a prophet, that he could give him an answer to the enquiry which he had not yet made, and tell him what he thought; and thence he might infer, if a man of God can do this, much more doth God himself <hi type="italic">understand our thoughts afar off.</hi> 3. He surprises him with an intimation of preferment before him: "<hi type="italic">On whom is all the desire of Israel?</hi> Is it not a king that they are set upon, and there is never a man in Israel that will suit them as thou wilt." It does not appear that the country had as yet any eye upon him for the government, because they had left it wholly to God to choose for them; but such a one as he they wished for, and his advancement would be the advancement of his family and relations, as Abner, and others. 4. To this strange intimation Saul returns a very modest answer, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.21">v. 21</reference>. Samuel, he thought, did but banter him, because he was a tall man, but a very unlikely man to be a king; for, though the historian says (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">v. 1</reference>) his father was a <hi type="italic">mighty man of power,</hi> yet he himself speaks diminishingly of his tribe and family. "Benjamin, the youngest of Jacob's sons, when grown up to be a man, was called a <hi type="italic">little one</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.44.20">Gen. xliv. 20</reference>); that tribe was diminished by the war of Gibeah; and <hi type="italic">I am a Benjamite, my family the least,</hi>" probably a younger house, not in any place of honour or trust, no, not in their own tribe. Gideon had expressed himself thus, <reference osisRef="Judg.6.15">Judg. vi. 15</reference>. A humble disposition is a good presage of preferment. <div eID="gen5421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5422" type="x-p"/> II. At the public feast; thither Samuel took him and his servant. Though the advancement of Saul would be the deposing of Samuel, yet that good prophet was so far from envying him, or bearing him any ill-will for it, that he was the first and forwardest man to do him honour, in compliance with the will of God. If this be the man whom God has chosen, though he be none of Samuel's particular friends or confidants, yet he is heartily welcome to his table, nay, to his bosom. We may suppose it was no unseasonable kindness to Saul to give him a meal's meat, for it seems, by what he said (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.7">v. 7</reference>), that all their meat and money were spent. But this was not all. Samuel treats him not as a common person, but a person of quality and distinction, to prepare both him and the people for what was to follow. Two marks of honour he put upon him:—1. He set him <hi type="italic">in the best place,</hi> as more honourable than any other of the guests, to whom he said, <hi type="italic">Give this man place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.14.9">Luke xiv. 9</reference>. Though we may suppose the magistrates were there, who in their own city would claim precedency, yet the master of the feast made Saul and his servant too (who, if Saul was a king, must be respected as his prime minister of state) <hi type="italic">sit in the chief place,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.22">v. 22</reference>. Note, Civil respects must be paid to those who in civil things have the precedency given them by the divine providence. 2. He presented him with the <hi type="italic">best dish,</hi> which, having had notice from heaven the day before of his coming (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.16">v. 16</reference>), he had designed for him, and ordered the cook to secure for him, when he gave orders for inviting the guests and making preparation for them. And what should this precious dish be, which was so very carefully reserved for the king-elect? One would expect it should be something very nice and delicate. No, it was a plain shoulder of mutton (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.23-1Sam.9.24">v. 23, 24</reference>). The right shoulder of the peace-offerings was to be given to the priests, who were God's receivers (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.32">Lev. vii. 32</reference>); the next in honour to that was the left shoulder, which probably was always allotted to those that sat at the upper end of the table, and was wont to be Samuel's mess at other times; so that his giving it to Saul now was an implicit resignation of his place to him. Some observe a significancy in this dish. The shoulder denotes strength, and the breast, which some think went with it, denotes affection: he that was king had <hi type="italic">the government upon his shoulder,</hi> for he must bear the weight of it; and the people in his bosom, for they must be dear to him. <div eID="gen5422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5423" type="x-p"/> III. What passed between them in private. Both that evening and early the next morning Samuel communed with Saul upon the flat roof of the house, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.25-1Sam.9.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. We may suppose Samuel now told him the whole story of the people's desire of a king, the grounds of their desire, and God's grant of it, to all which Saul, living very privately, was perhaps a stranger; he satisfied him that he was the person God had pitched upon for the government; and whereas Saul would object that Samuel was in possession, and he would not for all the world take it out of his hands, Samuel, we may suppose, gave him all the assurance he could desire of his willingness to resign. Early in the morning he sent him towards home, brought him part of the way, bade him send his servant before, that they might be private (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.27">v. 27</reference>), and there, as we find in the beginning of the next chapter, he anointed him, and therein showed him the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord,</hi> that is, gave him full satisfaction that he was the person chosen to be king, for he would not jest with that sacred rite. It is by the <hi type="italic">unction of the Holy Ghost</hi> that Christ, the great prophet, <hi type="italic">shows us the word of the Lord.</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.27">1 John ii. 27</reference>, <hi type="italic">the same anointing teacheth you of all things.</hi>  <chapter eID="1Sam.9"/> <div eID="gen5423" type="x-p"/>

entries.e8caf7b8ecfefcaff7cbcac8fe07acd8fd3b4df4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2567"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <div sID="gen3476" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1-1Sam.9.14">1Sa 9:1-14</reference>. Saul, Despairing to Find His Father's Asses, Comes to Samuel.<div eID="gen3476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3477" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2567"/><hi type="bold">1. a mighty man of power--</hi>that is, of great wealth and substance. The family was of high consideration in the tribe of Benjamin, and therefore Saul's words must be set down among the common forms of affected humility, which Oriental people are wont to use. <div eID="gen3477" type="x-p"/>
entries.363b02ce620720ae94b86e2277272f4c043c7952: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2568"/><div sID="gen3478" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2568"/><hi type="bold">2. Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly--</hi>He had a fine appearance; for it is evident that he must have been only a little under seven feet tall. A gigantic stature and an athletic frame must have been a popular recommendation at that time in that country. <div eID="gen3478" type="x-p"/>
entries.fffb5b1de746effeb7dbf74a8da32353b8609a5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2569"/><div sID="gen3479" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2569"/><hi type="bold">3. the asses of Kish Saul's father were lost. And Kish said to Saul ... arise, go seek the asses--</hi>The probability is that the family of Kish, according to the immemorial usage of Oriental shepherds in the purely pastoral regions, had let the animals roam at large during the grazing season, at the close of which messengers were despatched in search of them. Such travelling searches are common; and, as each owner has his own stamp marked on his cattle, the mention of it to the shepherds he meets gradually leads to the discovery of the strayed animals. This ramble of Saul's had nothing extraordinary in it, except its superior directions and issue, which turned its uncertainty into certainty. <div eID="gen3479" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ff69c98a34d9d1552fd908b75e132513f80f874: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2570"/><div sID="gen3480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2570"/><hi type="bold">4-5. he passed through mount Ephraim--</hi>This being situated on the north of Benjamin, indicates the direction of Saul's journey. The district explored means the whole of the mountainous region, with its valleys and defiles, which belonged to Ephraim. Turning apparently southwards--probably through the verdant hills between Shiloh and the vales of Jordan (Shalisha and Shalim)--he approached again the borders of Benjamin, scoured the land of Zuph, and was proposing to return, when his servant recollected that they were in the immediate neighborhood of the man of God, who would give them counsel. <div eID="gen3480" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b341ec35d7958d03da6eee87fde32aaa1163500: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2571"/><div sID="gen3481" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2571"/><hi type="bold">6. there is in this city a man of God--</hi>Ramah was the usual residence of Samuel, but several circumstances, especially the mention of Rachel's sepulchre, which lay in Saul's way homeward [1Sa 10:2], lead to the conclusion that "this city" was not the Ramah where Samuel dwelt.<div eID="gen3481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peradventure he can show us our way that we should go--</hi>It seems strange that a dignified prophet should be consulted in such an affair. But it is probable that at the introduction of the prophetic office, the seers had discovered things lost or stolen, and thus their power for higher revelations was gradually established. <div eID="gen3482" type="x-p"/>
entries.79f8141cf606d4703f4db446380ba33041a29608: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2572"/><div sID="gen3483" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2572"/><hi type="bold">7. Saul said to his servant, But, behold, if we go, what shall we bring the man?--</hi>According to Eastern notions, it would be considered a want of respect for any person to go into the presence of a superior man of rank or of official station without a present of some kind in his hand, however trifling in value.<div eID="gen3483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the bread is spent in our vessels--</hi>Shepherds, going in quest of their cattle, put up in a bag as much flour for making bread as will last sometimes for thirty days. It appears that Saul thought of giving the man of God a cake from his travelling bag, and this would have been sufficient to render the indispensable act of civility--the customary tribute to official dignity. <div eID="gen3484" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd83e01a53b4accc7d4b3cb002772109468dfd9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2573"/><div sID="gen3485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2573"/><hi type="bold">8. the fourth part of a shekel of silver--</hi>rather more than sixpence. Contrary to our Western notions, money is in the East the most acceptable form in which a present can be made to a man of rank. <div eID="gen3485" type="x-p"/>
entries.472d771060383b4e36f9c0ba9bb151e0707d0bf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2574"/><div sID="gen3486" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2574"/><hi type="bold">9. seer ... Prophet--</hi>The recognized distinction in latter times was, that a seer was one who was favored with visions of God--a view of things invisible to mortal sight; and a prophet foretold future events. <div eID="gen3486" type="x-p"/>
entries.dda7abaf7a95be61008120de14eaf380e2c63adf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2575"/><div sID="gen3487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2575"/><hi type="bold">11-13. as they went up the hill--</hi>The modern village, Er-Rameh, lies on an eminence; and on their way they met a band of young maidens going out to the well, which, like all similar places in Palestine, was beyond the precincts of the town. From these damsels they learned that the day was devoted to a festival occasion, in honor of which Samuel had arrived in the city; that a sacrifice had been offered, which was done by prophets in extraordinary circumstances at a distance from the tabernacle, and that a feast was to follow--implying that it had been a peace offering; and that, according to the venerable practice of the Israelites, the man of God was expected to ask a special blessing on the food in a manner becoming the high occasion. <div eID="gen3487" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1d4343a1464e5bdbd17e23393bcd4098f5b5746: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2576"/><div sID="gen3488" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2576"/><hi type="bold">14. Samuel came out against them, for to go up to the high place--</hi>Such were the simple manners of the times that this prophet, the chief man in Israel, was seen going to preside at a high festival undistinguished either by his dress or equipage from any ordinary citizen.<div eID="gen3488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3489" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15-1Sam.9.27">1Sa 9:15-27</reference>. God Reveals to Samuel Saul's Coming, and His Appointment to the Kingdom. <div eID="gen3489" type="x-p"/>
entries.d66b525b46dbec328ea0333bbefef8091ec411c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2577"/><div sID="gen3490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2577"/><hi type="bold">15-16. Now the Lord had told Samuel in his ear a day before--</hi>The description of Saul, the time of his arrival, and the high office to which he was destined, had been secretly intimated to Samuel from heaven. The future king of Israel was to fight the battles of the Lord and protect His people. It would appear that they were at this time suffering great molestation from the Philistines, and that this was an additional reason of their urgent demands for the appointment of a king (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1Sa 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.3">13:3</reference>). <div eID="gen3490" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfcb62a2bd92dc7ab3ddedfc810f487f2b4e96c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2578"/><div sID="gen3491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2578"/><hi type="bold">18-20. Tell me, I pray thee, where the seer's house is--</hi>Satisfying the stranger's inquiry, Samuel invited him to the feast, as well as to sojourn till the morrow; and, in order to reconcile him to the delay, he assured him that the strayed asses had been recovered. <div eID="gen3491" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a6c3696450d3a84aea65e958141652b79ac8c85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2581"/><div sID="gen3494" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2581"/><hi type="bold">22. Samuel took Saul and his servant, and brought them into the parlour--</hi>The toil-worn but noble-looking traveller found himself suddenly seated among the principal men of the place and treated as the most distinguished guest. <div eID="gen3494" type="x-p"/>
entries.74676b104b98d9b82376c4c93e9e19ec224a645d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2582"/><div sID="gen3495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2582"/><hi type="bold">24. the cook took up the shoulder ... and set it before Saul. And Samuel said, Behold that which is left; set it before thee, and eat--</hi>that is, reserved (see on <reference osisRef="Gen.18.7">Ge 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.34">Ge 43:34</reference>). This was, most probably, the right shoulder; which, as the perquisite of the sacrifice, belonged to Samuel, and which he had set aside for his expected guest. In the sculptures of the Egyptian shambles, also, the first joint taken off was always the right shoulder for the priest. The meaning of those distinguished attentions must have been understood by the other guests. <div eID="gen3495" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e1f0ddfe73068ee36318ede9fd8e5e4d9513ed7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2583"/><div sID="gen3496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2583"/><hi type="bold">25-27. Samuel communed with Saul upon the top of the house--</hi>Saul was taken to lodge with the prophet for that night. Before retiring to rest, they communed on the flat roof of the house, the couch being laid there (<reference osisRef="Josh.2.6">Jos 2:6</reference>), when, doubtless, Samuel revealed the secret and described the peculiar duties of a monarch in a nation so related to the Divine King as Israel. Next morning early, Samuel roused his guest, and conveying him on his way towards the skirts of the city, sought, before parting, a private interview--the object of which is narrated in the next chapter. <chapter eID="1Sam.9"/>

entries.4d57fe95f24800cb7105ce06f0f93d6b4abb1300: <div eID="gen9856" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen9857" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9858" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9858" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9857" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9859" type="x-p"/> Saul's lineage and description; he is sent by his father to seek some lost asses, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1-1Sam.9.5">1Sam 9:1-5</reference>. Not finding them, he purposes to go and consult Samuel concerning the proper method of proceeding, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6-1Sam.9.14">1Sam 9:6-14</reference>. The Lord informs Samuel that he should anoint Saul king, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15">1Sam 9:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.16">1Sam 9:16</reference>. Samuel invites Saul to dine with him, and informs him that the asses are found; and gives him an intimation that he is to be king, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.17-1Sam.9.21">1Sam 9:17-21</reference>. Saul dines with Samuel, and afterwards he is taken to the house-top, where both commune together, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.22-1Sam.9.27">1Sam 9:22-27</reference>. <div eID="gen9859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9860" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen9860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9861" type="x-p"/> A mighty man of power - Literally, a strong man; this appears to be the only power he possessed; and the physical strength of the father may account for the extraordinary size of the son. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.2">1Sam 9:2</reference>.
entries.e3408dfcefe10d7ed5e4ded0b7174dde2b251f2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen9861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9862" type="x-p"/> From his shoulders and upwards - It was probably from this very circumstance that he was chosen for king; for, where kings were elective, in all ancient times great respect was paid to personal appearance.
entries.444e97245d894c23af84f1a8fe72b82a7ac102ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen9862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9863" type="x-p"/> The asses of Kish - were lost - What a wonderful train of occurrences were connected in order to bring Saul to the throne of Israel! Every thing seems to go on according to the common course of events, and yet all conspired to favor the election of a man to the kingdom who certainly did not come there by the approbation of God. <div eID="gen9863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9864" type="x-p"/> Asses grow to great perfection in the East; and at this time, as there were no horses in Judea, they were very useful; and on them kings and princes rode.
entries.c91c694d07695849eb6153a682bca1df8bb09d4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen9864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9865" type="x-p"/> Were come to the land of Zuph - Calmet supposes that Saul and his servant went from Gibeah to Shalisha, in the tribe of Dan; from thence to Shalim, near to Jerusalem; and thence, traversing the tribe of Benjamin, they purposed to return to Gibeah; but passing through the land of Zuph, in which Ramatha, the country of Samuel, was situated, they determined to call on this prophet to gain some directions from him; the whole of this circuit he supposes to have amounted to no more than about twenty-five leagues, or three days' journey. We do not know where the places were situated which are here mentioned: the Targum translates thus: "And he passed through the mount of the house of Ephraim, and went into the southern land, but did not meet with them. And he passed through the land of Mathbera, but they were not there; and he passed through the land of the tribe of Benjamin, but did not find them; then they came into the land where the prophet of the Lord dwelt. And Saul said to his servant," etc.
entries.635071ed07ad1b03ae831aac8648e63b6aac93ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen9865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9866" type="x-p"/> There is not a present to bring to the man of God - We are not to suppose from this that the prophets took money to predict future events: Saul only refers to an invariable custom, that no man approached a superior without a present of some kind or other. We have often seen this before; even God, who needs nothing, would not that his people should approach him with empty hands. "It is very common in Bengal for a person, who is desirous of asking a favor from a superior, to take a present of fruits or sweetmeats in his hand. If not accepted, the feelings of the offerer are greatly wounded. The making of presents to appease a superior is also very common in Bengal." - Ward's Customs.
entries.d4427cd95adaf73d197eaded67825a3e82e2c125: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen9866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9867" type="x-p"/> The fourth part of a shekel of silver - We find from the preceding verse, that the bread or provisions which they had brought with them for their journey was expended, else a part of that would have been thought a suitable present; and here the fourth part of a shekel of silver, about ninepence of our money, was deemed sufficient: therefore the present was intended more as a token of respect than as an emolument.
entries.ac31486cebb5b4c40d660bfb0b5f789da511f894: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen9867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9868" type="x-p"/> Beforetime in Israel - This passage could not have been a part of this book originally: but we have already conjectured that Samuel, or some contemporary author, wrote the memoranda, out of which a later author compiled this book. This hypothesis, sufficiently reasonable in itself, solves all difficulties of this kind. <div eID="gen9868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9869" type="x-p"/> Was beforetime called a seer - The word seer, ראה roeh, occurs for the first time in this place; it literally signifies a person who Sees; particularly preternatural sights. A seer and a prophet were the same in most cases; only with this difference, the seer was always a prophet, but the prophet was not always a seer. A seer seems to imply one who frequently met with, and saw, some symbolical representation of God. The term prophet was used a long time before this; Abraham is called a prophet, <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen 20:7</reference>, and the term frequently occurs in the law. Besides, the word seer does not occur before this time; but often occurs afterwards down through the prophets, for more than three hundred years. See <reference osisRef="Amo.7.12">Amo 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.7">Mic 3:7</reference>. <div eID="gen9869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9870" type="x-p"/> All prophets, false and true, profess to see God; see the case of Balaam, <reference osisRef="Num.24.4">Num 24:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.16">Num 24:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.14.14">Jer 14:14</reference>. All diviners, in their enthusiastic flights, boasted that they had those things exhibited to their sight which should come to pass. There is a remarkable account in Virgil which may serve as a specimen of the whole; the Sibyl professes to be a seer: - - Bella, horrida bella, <div eID="gen9870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9871" type="x-p"/> Et Tyberim molto spumantem sanguine <div eID="gen9871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9872" type="x-p"/> Cerno. Aen. lib. vi., ver. 86. <div eID="gen9872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9873" type="x-p"/> Wars, horrid wars, I View; a field of blood; <div eID="gen9873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9874" type="x-p"/> And Tyber rolling with a purple flood. <div eID="gen9874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9875" type="x-p"/> I think the 9th verse comes more naturally in after the 11th.
entries.7bfa2992f0389eb578ba1ba82003120937dde415: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen9875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9876" type="x-p"/> Young maidens going out to draw water - So far is it from being true, that young women were always kept closely shut up at home, that we find them often in the field, drawing and carrying water, as here.
entries.fe6312809e83fcb9b4477e4a777613060e1915f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen9876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9877" type="x-p"/> He came to - day to the city - Though Samuel lived chiefly in Ramah, yet he had a dwelling in the country, at a place called Naioth, where it is probable there was a school of the prophets. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.18-1Sam.19.24">1Sam 19:18-24</reference>. <div eID="gen9877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9878" type="x-p"/> A sacrifice of the people - A great feast. The animals used were first sacrificed to the Lord; that is, their blood was poured out before him; and then all the people fed on the flesh. By high place probably Samuel's altar is alone meant; which no doubt was raised on an eminence.
entries.9cc543402945e609777a2b107cdd62d064efc8ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen9878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9879" type="x-p"/> He doth bless the sacrifice - He alone can perform the religious rites which are used on this occasion. <div eID="gen9879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9880" type="x-p"/> Afterwards they eat that be bidden - Among the Arabs, often a large feast is made of sacrificed camels, etc., and then the people of the vicinity are invited to come and partake of the sacrifice. This is the custom to which allusion is made here.
entries.1e15525319e1205dcf523217df1e3c47e901ab6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen9880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9881" type="x-p"/> Come out against them - Met them.
entries.a390410668079d71991be4b37fcdea132f11e126: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen9881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9882" type="x-p"/> Now the Lord had told Samuel - How this communication was made, we cannot tell.
entries.1ff435360637d15555a8bd4a4dfb6208bb6d3b97: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen9882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9883" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt anoint him to be captain - Not to be king, but to be נגיד nagid or captain of the Lord's host. But in ancient times no king was esteemed who was not an able warrior. Plutarch informs us that Alexander the Great esteemed the following verse the most correct, as to its sentiment, of any in the whole Iliad of Homer: - Ουτος γ' Ατρειδης ευρυκρειων Αγαμεμνων, Αμφοτερον βασιλευς τ' αγαθος, κρατερος τ' αιχμητης. "The king of kings, Atrides, you survey; <div eID="gen9883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9884" type="x-p"/> Great in the war, and great in acts of sway." <div eID="gen9884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9885" type="x-p"/> Pope.
entries.c0ab55a316d7fe4695e60e847c72b4d5cb70a27a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen9885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9886" type="x-p"/> Behold the man whom I spake to thee of - What an intimate communion must Samuel have held with his God! A constant familiarity seems to have existed between them.
entries.e53e552c8e2071ef300a4737ca861500990bcc54: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen9886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9887" type="x-p"/> I am the seer - This declaration would prepare Saul for the communications afterwards made.
entries.31140c7e233d5b3af749b7abdf8e4b2274ba16e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen9887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9888" type="x-p"/> As for thine asses - Thus he shows him that he knew what was in his heart, God having previously revealed these things to Samuel. <div eID="gen9888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9889" type="x-p"/> And on whom is all the desire of Israel? - Saul understood this as implying that he was chosen to be king.
entries.8958e12ee1e1c57960d517a6217e3da865605b66: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen9889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9890" type="x-p"/> Am not I a Benjamite - This speech of Saul is exceedingly modest; he was now becomingly humble; but who can bear elevation and prosperity? The tribe of Benjamin had not yet recovered its strength, after the ruinous war it had with the other tribes, Judges 20:29-46.
entries.8b30b0d797616c0042acddd780c7dd3cf22c06db: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen9890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9891" type="x-p"/> Brought them into the parlour - It might as well be called kitchen; it was the place where they sat down to feast.
entries.870d61f01d2fc00929b06c429d33cca0061a6af0: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen9891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9892" type="x-p"/> Said unto the cook - טבח tabbach, here rendered cook; the singular of טבחות tabbachoth, female cooks, <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.13">1Sam 8:13</reference>, from the root tabach, to slay or butcher. Probably the butcher is here meant.
entries.d5f54f6caae7d4569faf5fc67968d965b308f3f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen9892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9893" type="x-p"/> The shoulder, and that which was upon it - Probably the shoulder was covered with a part of the caul, that it might be the better roasted. The Targum has it the shoulder and its thigh; not only the shoulder merely, but the fore-leg bone to the knee; perhaps the whole fore-quarter. Why was the shoulder set before Saul? Not because it was the best part, but because it was an emblem of the government to which he was now called. See <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference> : And the government shall be upon his Shoulder.
entries.9a1547b68375a047488ec87b656bfffe9f358997: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen9893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9894" type="x-p"/> Upon the top of the house - All the houses in the East were flat-roofed; on these people walked, talked, and frequently slept, for the sake of fresh and cooling air.
entries.5ca841fb0d0a490d18abf980ab9ac3da06db015e: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen9894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9895" type="x-p"/> Called Saul to the top of the house - Saul had no doubt slept there all night; and now, it being the break of day, "Samuel called to Saul on the top of the house, saying, Up, that I may send thee away." There was no calling him to the house-top a second time he was sleeping there, and Samuel called him up.
entries.3c0c64c2c87688a17dfc8c0f9d12cf509b63dfb8: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen9895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9896" type="x-p"/> As they were going down - So it appears that Saul arose immediately, and Samuel accompanied him out of the town, and sent the servant on that he might show Saul the word, the counsel or design, of the Lord. What this was we shall see in the following chapter, 1 Samuel 10 (note).  <chapter eID="1Sam.9"/> <div eID="gen9896" type="x-p"/>

entries.ce87405de66bd0935da94e092400ae4919f1305e: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1-1Sam.9.2">1Sa 9:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">Saul searches for his father’s asses</hi>. - <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1">1Sa 9:1</reference>, 1Sa 9:2. The elaborate genealogy of the Benjaminite Kish, and the minute description of the figure of his son Saul, are intended to indicate at the very outset the importance to which Saul attained in relation to the people of Israel, <hi type="italic">Kish</hi> was the son of <hi type="italic">Abiel</hi>: this is in harmony with 1Sa 14:51. But when, on the other hand, it is stated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.33">1Ch 8:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.39">1Ch 9:39</reference>, that <hi type="italic">Ner</hi> begat <hi type="italic">Kish</hi>, the difference may be reconciled in the simplest manner, on the assumption that the <hi type="italic">Ner</hi> mentioned there is not the father, but the grandfather, or a still more remote ancestor of Kish, as the intervening members are frequently passed over in the genealogies. The other ancestors of <hi type="italic">Kish</hi> are never mentioned again. חיל גּבּור refers to <hi type="italic">Kish</hi>, and signifies not a brave man, but a man of property, as in Rth 2:1. This son <hi type="italic">Saul</hi> (i.e., “<hi type="italic">prayed for</hi>:” for this meaning of the word, comp. <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.17">1Sa 1:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.27">1Sa 1:27</reference>) was “<hi type="italic">young and beautiful</hi>.” It is true that even at that time Saul had a son grown up (viz., Jonathan), according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.2">1Sa 13:2</reference>; but still, in contrast with his father, he was “a young man,” i.e., in the full vigour of youth, probably about forty or forty-five years old. There is no necessity, therefore, to follow the Vulgate rendering <hi type="italic">electus</hi>. No one equalled him in beauty. “<hi type="italic">From his shoulder upwards he was higher than any of the people</hi>.” Such a figure as this was well adapted to commend him to the people as their king (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.24">1Sa 10:24</reference>), since size and beauty were highly valued in rulers, as signs of manly strength (see Herod. iii. 20, vii. 187; Aristot. <hi type="italic">Polit</hi>. iv. c. 24).
entries.5efadfed15eb9014a494784ab6e61b703b41bea5: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.3-1Sam.9.5">1Sa 9:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen3767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3768" type="x-p"/> Having been sent out by his father to search for his she-asses which had strayed, Saul went with his servant through the mountains of Ephraim, which ran southwards into the tribe-territory of Benjamin (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.1">1Sa 1:1</reference>), then through the land of Shalishah and the land of Shaalim, and after that through the land of Benjamin, without finding the asses; and at length, when he had reached the land of Zuph, he determined to return, because he was afraid that his father might turn his mind from the asses, and trouble himself about them (the son and servant). מן חדל, to desist from a thing, to give it up or renounce it. <div eID="gen3768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3769" type="x-p"/> As Saul started in any case from Gibeah of Benjamin, his own home (1Sa 10:10., <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.26">1Sa 10:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.4">1Sa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.34">1Sa 15:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">1Sa 23:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.1">1Sa 26:1</reference>), i.e., the present <hi type="italic">Tuleil el Phul</hi>, which was an hour or an hour and a half to the north of Jerusalem (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.28">Jos 18:28</reference>), and went thence into the mountains of Ephraim, he no doubt took a north-westerly direction, so that he crossed the boundary of Benjamin somewhere between Bireh and Atarah, and passing through the crest of the mountains of Ephraim, on the west of Gophnah (Jifna), came out into the land of Shalishah. <hi type="italic">Shalishah</hi> is unquestionably the country round (or of) <hi type="italic">Baal-shalishah</hi> (2Ki 4:42), which was situated, according to <hi type="italic">Eusebius</hi> (<hi type="italic">Onom. s.v</hi>. Βαιθσαρισάθ: <hi type="italic">Beth-sarisa</hi> or <hi type="italic">Beth-salisa</hi>), <hi type="italic">in regione Thamnitica</hi>, fifteen Roman miles to the north of Diospolis (Lydda), and was therefore probably the country to the west of Jiljilia, where three different wadys run into one large wady, called Kurawa; and according to the probable conjecture of Thenius, it was from this fact that the district received the name of <hi type="italic">Shalishah</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Three-land</hi>. They proceeded thence in their search to the land of <hi type="italic">Shaalim</hi>: according to the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. (<hi type="italic">s.v.</hi>), “a village seven miles off, <hi type="italic">in finibus Eleutheropoleos contra occidentem</hi>.” But this is hardly correct, and is most likely connected with the mistake made in transposing the town of Samuel to the neighbourhood of Diospolis (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.1">1Sa 1:1</reference>). For since they went on from Shaalim into the land of Benjamin, and then still further into the land of Zuph, on the south-west of Benjamin, they probably turned eastwards from Shalishah, into the country where we find <hi type="italic">Beni Mussah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Beni Salem</hi> marked upon <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>'s and v. de Velde’s maps, and where we must therefore look for the land of <hi type="italic">Shaalim</hi>, that they might proceed thence to explore the land of Benjamin from the north-east to the south-west. If, on the contrary, they had gone from Shaalim in a southerly or south-westerly direction, to the district of Eleutheropolis, they would only have entered the land of Benjamin at the south-west corner, and would have had to go all the way back again in order to go thence to the land of Zuph. For we may infer with certainty that the land of Zuph was on the south-west of the tribe-territory of Benjamin, from the fact that, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>, Saul and his companion passed Rachel’s tomb on their return thence to their own home, and then came to the border of Benjamin. On the name <hi type="italic">Zuph</hi>, see at 1Sa 1:1.
entries.84a1fdf617cb8a76d2400733bab7488baff8eb30: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6">1Sa 9:6</reference> <div eID="gen3769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3770" type="x-p"/> When Saul proposed to return home from the land of Zuph, his servant said to him, “<hi type="italic">Behold, in this city</hi> (<hi type="italic">'this</hi>,' referring to the town which stood in front of them upon a hill) <hi type="italic">is a man of God, much honoured; all that he saith cometh surely to pass: now we will go thither; perhaps he will tell us our way that we have to go</hi>” (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. have gone, and still go, sc., to attain the object of our journey, viz., to find the asses). The name of this town is not mentioned either here or in the further course of this history. Nearly all the commentators suppose it to have been Ramah, Samuel’s home. But this assumption has no foundation at all in the text, and is irreconcilable with the statements respecting the return in <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>-5. The servant did not say there <hi type="italic">dwells</hi> in this city, but there is in this city (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6">1Sa 9:6</reference>; comp. with this <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.10">1Sa 9:10</reference>, “They went into the city where the man of God was,” not “dwelt”). It is still more evident, from the answer given by the drawers of water, when Saul asked them, “<hi type="italic">Is the seer here?</hi>” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.11">1Sa 9:11</reference>), - viz., “<hi type="italic">He came to-day to the city, for the people have a great sacrifice upon the high place</hi>” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.12">1Sa 9:12</reference>), - that the seer (Samuel) did not live in the town, but had only come thither to a sacrificial festival. Moreover, “every impartial man will admit, that the fact of Samuel’s having honoured Saul as his guest at the sacrificial meal of those who participated in the sacrifice, and of their having slept under the same roof, cannot possibly weaken the impression that Samuel was only there in his peculiar and official capacity. It could not be otherwise than that the presidency should be assigned to him at the feast itself as priest and prophet, and therefore that the appointments mentioned should proceed from him. And it is but natural to assume that he had a house at his command for any repetition of such sacrifices, which we find from 2 Kings 4 to have been the case in the history of Elisha” (Valentiner). And lastly, the sacrificial festival itself does not point to Ramah; for although Samuel had built an altar to the Lord at Ramah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.17">1Sa 7:17</reference>), this was by no means the only place of sacrifice in the nation. If Samuel offered sacrifice at Mizpeh and Gilgal (<reference osisRef="1Sam.7.9">1Sa 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.8">1Sa 10:8</reference>; 1Sa 13:8.), he could also do the same at other places. What the town really was in which Saul met with him, cannot indeed be determined, since all that we can gather from <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>, is, that it was situated on the south-west of Bethlehem.
entries.1426d97809da85249424b4849f70be2df4fdb432: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.7-1Sam.9.8">1Sa 9:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen3770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3771" type="x-p"/> Saul’s objection, that they had no present to bring to the man of God, as the bread was gone from their vessels, was met by the servant with the remark, that he had a quarter of a shekel which he would give.
entries.08498dd8dc0568b249011080abc96353d14bdb39: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.9-1Sam.9.10">1Sa 9:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen3771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3772" type="x-p"/> Before proceeding with the further progress of the affair, the historian introduces a notice, which was required to throw light upon what follows; namely, that beforetime, if any one wished to inquire of God, i.e., to apply to a prophet for counsel from God upon any matter, it was customary in Israel to say, We will go to the seer, because “<hi type="italic">he that is now called a prophet was beforetime called a seer</hi>.” After this parenthetical remark, the account is continued in 1Sa 9:10. Saul declared himself satisfied with the answer of the servant; and they both went into the town, to ask the man of God about the asses that were lost.
entries.cfbf2f6bb02ef088208ee694e93b6c3d5db31d5c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.11-1Sam.9.12">1Sa 9:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen3772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3773" type="x-p"/> As they were going up to the high place of the town, they met maidens coming out of the town to draw water; and on asking them whether the seer was there, they received this answer: “<hi type="italic">Yes; behold, he is before thee: make haste, now, for he has come into the town to-day; for the people have a sacrifice to-day upon the high place</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Bamah</hi> (in the singular) does not mean the height or hill generally; but throughout it signifies <hi type="italic">the high place</hi>, as a place of sacrifice or prayer.
entries.802aa893080d4747dd688e1184fcfded25687a58: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.13">1Sa 9:13</reference> <div eID="gen3773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3774" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">When ye come into the city, ye will find him directly before he goes up to the high place to eat</hi>.” כּן not only introduces the apodosis, but corresponds to כּ, <hi type="italic">as</hi>, so: here, however, it is used with reference to time, in the sense of our “immediately.” “<hi type="italic">For the people are not accustomed to eat till he comes, for he blesses the sacrifice</hi>,” etc. בּרך, like εὐλογεῖν, refers to the thanksgiving prayer offered before the sacrificial meal. “<hi type="italic">Go now for him; yet will meet him even to-day</hi>.” The first אתו is placed at the beginning for the sake of emphasis, and then repeated at the close. כּהיּום, “<hi type="italic">Even to-day</hi>.”
entries.96ebeaea50abca693c7e5f459d8b174d4291275b: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.14-1Sam.9.16">1Sa 9:14-16</reference> <div eID="gen3774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3775" type="x-p"/> When they went into the town, Samuel met them on his way out to go to the high place of sacrifice. Before the meeting itself is described, the statement is introduced in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15-1Sam.9.17">1Sa 9:15-17</reference>, that the day before Jehovah had foretold to Samuel that the man was coming to him whom he was to anoint as captain over his people. אזן גּלה, to <hi type="italic">open any one’s ear</hi>, equivalent to <hi type="italic">reveal</hi> something to him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.12">1Sa 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.27">2Sa 7:27</reference>, etc.). אשׁלח, <hi type="italic">I will send thee</hi>, i.e., “I will so direct his way in my overruling providence, that he shall come to thee” (J. H. Mich. ). The words, “<hi type="italic">that he may save my people out of the hand of the Philistines; for I have looked upon my people, for their cry is come unto me</hi>,” are not at all at variance with 1Sa 7:13. In that passage there is simply the assertion, that there was no more any permanent oppression on the part of the Philistines in the days of Samuel, such as had taken place before; but an attempt to recover their supremacy over Israel is not only not precluded, but is even indirectly affirmed (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.13">1Sa 7:13</reference>).
