The words before us simply show that the Philistines had then begun to make a fresh attempt to contend for dominion over the Israelites. “<hi type="italic">I have looked upon my people</hi>:” this is to be explained like the similar passage in <reference osisRef="Exod.2.25">Exo 2:25</reference>, “God looked upon the children of Israel,” and <reference osisRef="Exod.3.7">Exo 3:7</reference>, “I have looked upon the misery of my people.” God’s looking was not a quiet, inactive looking on, but an energetic look, which brought help in trouble. “<hi type="italic">Their cry is come unto me</hi>:” this is word for word the same as in Exo 3:9. As the Philistines wanted to tread in the footsteps of the Egyptians, it was necessary that Jehovah should also send His people a deliverer from these new oppressors, by giving them a king. The reason here assigned for the establishment of a monarchy is by no means at variance with the displeasure which God had expressed to Samuel at the desire of the people for a king (1Sa 8:7.); since this displeasure had reference to the state of heart from which the desire had sprung.
entries.eb7b6ee78f2084d64ddb0532797ad812124f6cfa: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.17">1Sa 9:17</reference> <div eID="gen3775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3776" type="x-p"/> When Samuel saw Saul, the Lord answered him, sc., in reply to the tacit inquiry, <hi type="italic">'Is this he?</hi>' “<hi type="italic">Behold, this is the man of whom I spake to thee</hi>.” עצר, <hi type="italic">coercere imperio</hi>.
entries.9520b8ad41fe6ad4f9bd53e4373ed526fa8dce28: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.18-1Sam.9.24">1Sa 9:18-24</reference> <div eID="gen3776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3777" type="x-p"/> The thread of the narrative, which was broken off in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15">1Sa 9:15</reference>, is resumed in 1Sa 9:18. Saul drew near to Samuel in the gate, and asked him for the seer’s house. The expression השּׁער בּתוך is used to define more precisely the general phrase in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.14">1Sa 9:14</reference>, העיר בּתוך בּאים; and there is no necessity to alter העיר in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.14">1Sa 9:14</reference> into השּׁער, as Thenius proposes, for העיר בּתוך כּוא does not mean to go (or be) in the middle of the town, as he imagines, but to go <hi type="italic">into</hi>, or enter, <hi type="italic">the town</hi>; and the entrance to the town was through the gate.
entries.76b5ad7376f3c78da633aec347df9f70d538629a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.25-1Sam.9.27">1Sa 9:25-27</reference> <div eID="gen3780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3781" type="x-p"/> When the sacrificial meal was over, Samuel and Saul went down from the high place into the town, and he (Samuel) talked with him upon the roof (of the house into which Samuel had entered). The flat roofs of the East were used as placed of retirement for private conversation (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.22.8">Deu 22:8</reference>). This conversation did not refer of course to the call of Samuel to the royal dignity, for that was not made known to him as a word of Jehovah till the following day (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.27">1Sa 9:27</reference>); but it was intended to prepare him for that announcement: so that <hi type="italic">O. v. Gerlach</hi>'s conjecture is probably the correct one, viz., that Samuel “talked with Saul concerning the deep religious and political degradation of the people of God, the oppression of the heathen, the causes of the inability of the Israelites to stand against these foes, the necessity for a conversion of the people, and the want of a leader who was entirely devoted to the Lord.”<note placement="foot">For הגּג על עם־שׁאוּל וידבּר the lxx have καὶ διέστρωσαν τῷ Σαοὺλ ἐπι τῷ δώματι καὶ ἐκοιμήθη, “they prepared Saul a bed upon the house, and he slept,” from which Clericus conjectured that these translators had read לשאול וירבדו (וירבּדוּ or ויּרבּדוּ); and <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> and Thenius propose to alter the Hebrew text in this way. But although וגו ויּשׁכּימוּ (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.26">1Sa 9:26</reference>) no doubt presupposes that Saul had slept in Samuel’s house, and in fact upon the roof, the remark of Thenius, “that the private conversation upon the roof (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.25">1Sa 9:25</reference>) comes too early, as Saul did not yet know, and was not to learn till the following day, what was about to take place,” does not supply any valid objection to the correctness of the Masoretic text, or any argument in favour of the Septuagint rendering or interpretation, since it rests upon an altogether unfounded and erroneous assumption, viz., that Samuel had talked with Saul about his call to the throne. Moreover, “the strangeness” of the statement in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.26">1Sa 9:26</reference>, “they rose up early,” and then “when the morning dawned, Samuel called,” etc., cannot possibly throw any suspicion upon the integrity of the Hebrew text, as this “strangeness” vanishes when we take וגו כּעלות ויהי as a more precise definition of ויּשׁכּימוּ. The Septuagint translators evidently held the same opinion as their modern defenders. They took offence at Samuel’s private conversation with Saul, because he did not make known to him the word of God concerning his call to the throne till the next morning; and, on the other hand, as their rising the next morning is mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.26">1Sa 9:26</reference>, they felt the absence of any allusion to their sleeping, and consequently not only interpreted ידבר by a conjectural emendation as standing for ירבד rof, because מרבדּים רבד is used in <reference osisRef="Prov.7.16">Pro 7:16</reference> to signify the spreading of mats or carpets for a bed, but also identified וישׁכמו with ישׁכבו, and rendered it ἐκοιμήθη. At the same time, they did not reflect that the preparation of the bed and their sleeping during the night were both of them matters of course, and there was consequently no necessity to mention them; whereas Samuel’s talking with Saul upon the roof was a matter of importance in relation to the whole affair, and one which could not be passed over in silence. Moreover, the correctness of the Hebrew text is confirmed by all the other ancient versions. Not only do the Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic follow the Masoretic text, but <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> does the same in the rendering adopted by him, “<hi type="italic">Et locutus est cum Saule in solario. Cumque mane surrexissent;</hi>” though the words “<hi type="italic">stravitque Saul in solario et dormivit</hi>” have been interpolated probably from the Itala into the text of the Vulgate which has come down to us.</note>

                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And the asses of Kish, Saul's father, were lost: and Kish said to Saul his Son, Take now one of the servants with thee, and arise, go seek the asses <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which were there of great price and use, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 10. 4. and 12. 14. because of the scarcity of Horses, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 17. 16. and therefore not held unworthy of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s seeking, at least in those Ancient Times, when Simplicity, Humility and In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dustry, were in fashion among Persons of Quality.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And he passed through mount Ephraim <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">A part of the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Ephraim,</ns0:hi> which Bordered upon <ns0:hi>Benjamin;</ns0:hi> and therefore they could soon pass out of the one into the other, and back again, as they saw cause.</ns0:note>, and passed through the land of Shalisha, but they found <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> not: then they passed through the land of Shalim, and <ns0:hi>there they were</ns0:hi> not: and he passed through the land <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And he said unto him, Behold now, <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> in this city a man of God <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">A Prophet, as that Phrase is used, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 27. <ns0:hi>I<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And they answered them, and said, He is: behold, <ns0:hi>he is</ns0:hi> before you, make haste now: for he came to day to the city <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">She so speaks, though this was his own constant habi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation, because he had been travelling abroad, possibly in his Circuit, described 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 16, 17. and was now return<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to his own House in <ns0:hi>Ramah,</ns0:hi> as he used to do, and so she implies they come in a good and seasonable time to meet with him.</ns0:note>; for <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> a <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
